name: Natural law and natural human equality
plain_explanation: The Stoics argued that, beneath the different laws and customs of different nations (positive/conventional law), there exists a single universal law grounded in reason itself, which all rational beings share equally -- meaning that, by nature, all human beings (Greek or barbarian, free or slave) are fundamentally equal.
precise_definition: The Stoic distinction between jus naturale (natural law, derived from universally self-evident rational first principles held by all mankind) and jus gentium (the actual, variable laws and customs of particular peoples), together with the corollary doctrine that all human beings are equal by nature.
why_it_mattered: Russell identifies this as one of the two lasting, non-ethical-narrow contributions of Stoicism to later thought (the other being epistemology): it influenced Roman legislation (improving the legal status of women and slaves), was absorbed wholesale by Christianity, and was revived, in Christian dress, by seventeenth-century natural-rights theorists combating royal despotism.
historical_origin: Developed across the history of the school and stated explicitly by Marcus Aurelius, who favours 'a polity in which there is the same law for all... and equal freedom of speech.'
associated_philosopher: Marcus Aurelius (quoted); developed by the school generally
examples: Epictetus, a former slave, teaching that slaves are equal to other men as sons of God
Marcus Aurelius's stated ideal of 'a kingly government which respects most of all the freedom of the governed'
influence_on_later_thinkers: Christianity absorbed this doctrine; it re-emerged with 'practical force' in seventeenth-century natural-rights theory used to combat despotism, in Christian dress.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: This concept is explicitly political and directly informs Roman legal reform.
